questions.question: A standings report must give tied scores the same position while the next position skips the tied slots — producing 1, 1, 3 for scores 90, 90, 80. Which window function produces this numbering?
questions.explanation: RANK() assigns equal values the same rank and then skips as many positions as there were ties, so after two rank-1 rows the next row is rank 3.

questions.question: A second report must give tied scores the same position but continue the numbering with no gaps — producing 1, 1, 2 for scores 90, 90, 80. Which window function produces this numbering?
questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK() assigns equal values the same rank but never skips a number, so after two rank-1 rows the next row is rank 2.

questions.question: A salary ranking must restart at 1 within each department rather than rank the whole company — the OVER clause needs the sub-clause that splits rows into per-department groups. Which is it?
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY divides the input into separate window groups, so the ranking function re-executes independently inside each department's partition.

questions.question: A revenue report must show each month's figure beside the previous month's figure in the same output row, without writing a self-join. Which window function reads the prior row's value?
questions.explanation: LAG(col) fetches the value of col from the row a given offset before the current row in the ordered partition — offset 1 gives the previous month.

questions.question: The same report needs each month's figure beside the following month's figure — reading one row forward in the ordered partition. Which window function does this?
questions.explanation: LEAD(col) fetches the value of col from a row a given offset after the current row, mirroring LAG for forward-looking comparisons.

questions.question: For every row of a department, a report must repeat the salary of that department's top-paid employee — the value found in the first row of the ordered partition. Which window function returns it?
questions.explanation: FIRST_VALUE(col) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) returns the partition's first value — the maximum salary — on every row of that department.

questions.question: With the window frame extended to include UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, a query stamps each row with the value found in the final row of its ordered partition. Which window function returns it?
questions.explanation: LAST_VALUE(col) returns the last row's value in the frame; the frame must run to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING or the default frame ends at the current row.

questions.question: An uncorrelated subquery inside IN(...) would otherwise be re-evaluated for every outer row; instead the optimizer executes it once, stores the result in a temporary table, and reuses it. What is this strategy called?
questions.explanation: Materialization caches the subquery result as a temporary relation so it is computed once rather than once per outer row — a common optimizer rewrite for IN subqueries.

questions.question: WHERE salary > ALL(subquery) requires salary to exceed every returned value. A colleague rewrites it so the condition need only hold for at least one returned value — which operator does he use?
questions.explanation: ANY (synonym SOME) is satisfied when the comparison holds for at least one subquery result, in contrast to ALL which requires it to hold for every result.

questions.question: HR must label 400 employees, ordered by salary, into four pay bands numbered 1 through 4 of roughly equal size. Which window function assigns the band numbers?
questions.explanation: NTILE(4) splits the ordered rows into four buckets as evenly as possible, assigning each row its bucket number — quartiles for the pay-band analysis.

questions.question: A scalar subquery comparing each employee's salary to the company-wide average is written WHERE salary > ( ______ AVG(salary) FROM employees ) and fails with a syntax error. Which single keyword fills the blank?
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery needs its own SELECT to compute the average: WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees).

questions.question: The query SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 fails because WHERE cannot test aggregates. Which clause keyword must replace WHERE here?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups afterward, so aggregate conditions like COUNT(*) > 5 belong in HAVING.

questions.question: SELECT name, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) ranks the whole company, but the requirement is to restart the ranking inside each department — OVER (______ BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC). Which keyword fills the blank?
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY inside OVER restarts the window function for each distinct department, so every department gets its own rank-1 employee.

questions.question: A WITH query must walk an org chart by referencing itself inside its own definition; in standard SQL this self-referencing form requires one specific keyword after WITH. Which keyword?
questions.explanation: WITH RECURSIVE permits the CTE to reference its own name in the recursive member, enabling iteration over hierarchies until no new rows appear.

questions.question: Migrating MySQL's LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10 to standard SQL gives SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY id OFFSET 10 ROWS FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ______. Which keyword completes the clause?
questions.explanation: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY is the standard row-limiting clause; WITH TIES would instead include extra rows equal to the last fetched row.

questions.question: Employees have salaries 100, 100, and 90. Under RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC), what rank does the employee earning 90 receive?
questions.explanation: RANK gives tied rows the same rank and leaves gaps: the two 100s are rank 1 and the 90 is rank 3 (no rank 2).

questions.question: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY txn_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) produces what value for each row?
questions.explanation: The frame covers all rows from the partition start through the current row, so the sum accumulates — a running (cumulative) total.

questions.question: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY score) is applied to 9 rows. How many rows land in the first group?
questions.explanation: NTILE splits 9 rows into 4 buckets, giving the remainder (1 extra row) to the earliest groups: sizes are 3, 2, 2, 2.

questions.question: A recursive CTE is defined as: WITH RECURSIVE org AS (SELECT id, name FROM emp WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name FROM emp e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id). The first SELECT, executed once to seed the recursion, is called what?
questions.explanation: The anchor member produces the initial result set (here, top-level managers); the recursive member after UNION ALL iterates until it yields no more rows.

questions.question: SELECT a FROM t1 WHERE a NOT IN (SELECT b FROM t2) returns zero rows even though t1 clearly has values not present in t2. What must t2's column b contain?
questions.explanation: A NULL in the subquery makes every comparison UNKNOWN, so NOT IN returns no rows — a classic pitfall; NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe.
